steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a multimodal deep learning architecture that detects smoking-related content in text and images with little training data. Motivate it with the health impact of smoking and media influence, and survey the relevant text and image methods.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Smoking as a health problem and the influence of media
- Ways to identify smoking-related content; AI in tobacco research
- Data requirements of modern models
- Text and image methods for content identification
- Our proposal: multimodal architecture with pre-trained models

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Health and media
  - WHO: smoking causes around 8 million deaths a day
  - leading cause of death from many diseases: heart attacks, obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory diseases, cancers
  - 15% of people aged 15+ smoke in OECD countries, 17% in the European Union
  - 15% of the 8 million daily deaths from passive smoking
  - studies: smoking portrayal in movies, health communication models
  - quantifying media influence complex; no precise ad statistics for social sites; incited and unmarked ads hard to calculate
  - knowing smoking-related content in services -> tool to reduce popularity of smoking
- Identification methods
  - continuous monitoring of advertising intensity
  - structured data from questionnaires
  - AI-based solutions
  - review "Machine learning applications in tobacco research": AI powerful for tobacco control research and policy-making; researchers encouraged to explore
- Data intensity
  - ResNet trained on ImageNet, 14,197,122 images
  - BERT trained on 4.5 GB of Toronto BookCorpus
  - GPT models larger, more data; GPT 3.0 on CommonCrawl, 570 GB
- Methods
  - text: topic modeling; embeddings of words, tokens, sentences, characters; clustering; named-entity recognition
  - images: classification, object detection
  - popular models: VGG, ResNet, Xception, EfficientNet, Inception, YOLO
  - CAMFFNet specifically recommended for smoking detection
  - multimodal models: texts + images at once
  - movies: scene recognition harder than images
  - scene recognition for fire, smoke, disaster detection; point-of-sale and tobacco marketing practices
- Proposal
  - no public smoking dataset big enough to train from scratch
  - multimodal architecture, pre-trained image + language models
  - text and image data together; data-efficient, robust, improvable with expert input
  - AI/deep learning for covert advertising detection; unbiased, replicable, equitable quantification

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The WHO estimates at the moment that smoking causes around 8 million deaths a day. Smoking is the leading cause of death from a wide range of diseases, like heart attacks, obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory diseases and cancers. In the OECD countries 15% of people aged 15 years and over smoke, and in the European Union it is 17%. Also, 15% of the 8 million daily deaths come from passive smoking. The studies below show the influence of how smoking is portrayed in movies and how effective health communication models are. But it is complex to quantify the influence of media. For internet media like social sites there are no precise ad statistics. Calculating incited and unmarked ads is also a big difficulty. So knowing accurately what smoking-related content appears in individual services can be an effective tool to reduce the popularity of smoking. Methods to identify content include continuous monitoring of how intense advertising is, structured data that questionnaires generate, and AI-based solutions that can support these goals effectively. In their review, the authors of the article "Machine learning applications in tobacco research" point out that artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that can advance tobacco control research and policy-making. So researchers are encouraged to explore more possibilities.

But these methods need a lot of data. For image processing, a good example is the popular ResNet image processing network, which was trained on the ImageNet dataset with 14,197,122 images. For text processing, the popular and pioneering BERT network was trained on the 4.5 GB of Toronto BookCorpus. Generative text processing models like GPT are even bigger and were trained with a lot more data than BERT. For example, GPT 3.0 was trained on the CommonCrawl dataset, which is 570 GB.

- Methods for content identification
  - text: topic modeling; embeddings of words, tokens, sentences, characters; clustering; named-entity recognition
  - images: classification, object detection; VGG, ResNet, Xception, EfficientNet, Inception, YOLO; CAMFFNet for smoking detection
  - multimodal models (texts + images); movie scene recognition harder; fire/smoke/disaster detection; point-of-sale and tobacco marketing
- Proposal
  - no public smoking dataset sufficient to train from scratch
  - multimodal architecture with pre-trained image + language models; data-efficient, robust, expert input
  - covert advertising detection; unbiased, replicable, equitable quantification

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The WHO estimates at the moment that smoking causes around 8 million deaths a day. Smoking is the leading cause of death from a wide range of diseases, like heart attacks, obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory diseases and cancers. In the OECD countries 15% of people aged 15 years and over smoke, and in the European Union it is 17%. Also, 15% of the 8 million daily deaths come from passive smoking. The studies below show the influence of how smoking is portrayed in movies and how effective health communication models are. But it is complex to quantify the influence of media. For internet media like social sites there are no precise ad statistics. Calculating incited and unmarked ads is also a big difficulty. So knowing accurately what smoking-related content appears in individual services can be an effective tool to reduce the popularity of smoking. Methods to identify content include continuous monitoring of how intense advertising is, structured data that questionnaires generate, and AI-based solutions that can support these goals effectively. In their review, the authors of the article "Machine learning applications in tobacco research" point out that artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that can advance tobacco control research and policy-making. So researchers are encouraged to explore more possibilities.

But these methods need a lot of data. For image processing, a good example is the popular ResNet image processing network, which was trained on the ImageNet dataset with 14,197,122 images. For text processing, the popular and pioneering BERT network was trained on the 4.5 GB of Toronto BookCorpus. Generative text processing models like GPT are even bigger and were trained with a lot more data than BERT. For example, GPT 3.0 was trained on the CommonCrawl dataset, which is 570 GB.

Effective tools to identify the content of natural language texts are topic modeling and the embedding of words, tokens, sentences or characters, and clustering. To identify the content elements of texts more precisely we can use named-entity recognition techniques. In image processing, classification and object detection can be used to detect smoking. The most popular image processing models are VGG, ResNet, Xception, EfficientNet, Inception and YOLO. There are also architectures like CAMFFNet which are recommended specifically for smoking detection. Multimodal models, which can use texts and images to solve the tasks at the same time, are also getting more and more focus. For movies, scene recognition is especially challenging compared to images. Scene recognition is also connected to sensitive events like fire, smoke or other disaster detection systems, but there are also attempts to investigate point-of-sale and tobacco marketing practices.

We concluded that right now there is no publicly available dataset specific to smoking that would be enough to train a complex model from scratch. So we propose a multimodal architecture that uses pre-trained image and language models to detect smoking-related content in text and images. We combine image processing networks with multimodal architectures and language models, so we use textual and image data at the same time. This gives a solution that is data-efficient and robust and that can be improved further with expert input. This paper shows the remarkable potential of artificial intelligence, especially deep learning, for detecting covert advertising, and also its capacity to give unbiased, replicable and equitable quantification of media content related to tobacco.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The WHO currently estimates that smoking causes around 8 million deaths a day. It is the leading cause of death from a wide range of diseases, for example heart attacks, obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory diseases, and cancers. 15% of people aged 15 years and over smoke in the OECD countries, and 17% in the European Union [1]. Moreover, 15% of the 8 million daily deaths result from passive smoking [2]. The studies [3,4] below highlight the influence of smoking portrayal in movies and the effectiveness of health communication models. However, quantifying media influence is complex: for internet media such as social sites, precise ad statistics are unavailable, and calculating incited and unmarked ads is a significant difficulty as well. Accurate knowledge of the smoking-related content appearing in individual services can therefore be an effective tool for reducing the popularity of smoking. Methods for identifying such content include continuous monitoring of advertising intensity [5], structured data generated by questionnaires [6], and AI-based solutions that can effectively support these goals. In their review, the authors of the article "Machine learning applications in tobacco research" [7] point out that artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that can advance tobacco control research and policy-making, and researchers are therefore encouraged to explore further possibilities.

Nonetheless, these methods are highly data-intensive. In image processing, an excellent example is the popular ResNet [8] network, which was trained on the ImageNet dataset [9] containing 14,197,122 images. In text processing, the popular and pioneering BERT network [10] was trained on the 4.5 GB of Toronto BookCorpus [11]. Generative text processing models such as GPT [12] are even larger and were trained with significantly more data than BERT; for instance, the training set of GPT 3.0 was the CommonCrawl [13] dataset, with a size of 570 GB.

Effective tools for identifying the content of natural language texts are topic modeling [14] and the embedding of words [15,16,17], tokens, sentences [18], or characters [19], together with clustering [20]. For more precise identification of the content elements of texts, named-entity recognition [21] techniques can be used. In image processing, classification and object detection stand out for detecting smoking. The most popular image processing models are VGG [22], ResNet [8], Xception [23], EfficientNet [24], Inception [25], and YOLO [26], and there are architectures such as CAMFFNet [27] that are specifically recommended for smoking detection. Multimodal models, which can use texts and images to solve tasks at the same time, are also gaining increasing focus [28,29]. For movies, scene recognition is particularly challenging compared to images [30]. Scene recognition is also linked to sensitive events such as fire, smoke, or other disaster detection systems [31], but there are attempts to investigate point-of-sale and tobacco marketing practices [32] as well.

We concluded that there is currently no publicly available smoking-specific dataset sufficient to train a complex model from scratch. Hence, we propose a multimodal architecture that uses pre-trained image and language models to detect smoking-related content in text and images. By combining image processing networks with multimodal architectures and language models, we leverage textual and image data simultaneously, offering a data-efficient and robust solution that can be further improved with expert input. This paper demonstrates the remarkable potential of artificial intelligence, especially deep learning, for detecting covert advertising, along with its capacity to provide unbiased, replicable, and equitable quantification of tobacco-related media content.
